questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: What is the alternative medical eponym for hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.exp: The header explicitly notes: 'AKA Porto systemic encephalopathy.' (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: Match each type of hepatic encephalopathy with its underlying etiology — 1) Type A 2) Type B 3) Type C … A) Cirrhosis with portal hypertension (most common overall) B) Fulminant hepatic failure producing HE, where cerebral edema is the most common cause of death C) Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) associated HE
questions.exp: Classification: Type A = Fulminant failure (cerebral edema m/c cause of death); Type B = TIPSS-associated; Type C = Cirrhosis with Portal HTN (m/c). (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: What is the most common cause of death in patients with Type A hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.exp: Under Type A, the book notes: '↑ Cerebral edema : m/c cause of death'. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: Which of the following neurotoxins is NOT listed under the etiology of hepatic encephalopathy on this page?
questions.exp: Neurotoxins listed are NH3 (m/c), mercaptan, phenol, aromatic AA, Mn, GABA, octopamine, and free fatty acids; beta-amyloid is not listed. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: Fill up: In the colon, high dietary protein intake is converted into glutamine, which is subsequently converted into ammonia by the bacterial enzyme ______.
questions.exp: The flowchart notes that colonic bacteria metabolize glutamine via 'Glutaminase' to produce NH3. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: By which biophysical mechanism does gaseous ammonia (NH3) cross the blood-brain barrier to enter the brain?
questions.exp: The pathophysiology diagram states: 'NH3 ↑↑ Absorbed by : Non-ionic diffusion damages'. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: What characteristic histopathological astrocyte alteration is observed in hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.exp: Astrocytes in HE characteristically transform into 'Alzheimer's type-2 astrocyte'. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: Fill up: Inside astrocytes, ammonia and glutamate are combined by the enzyme ______ to form toxic glutamine, leading to osmotic astrocyte swelling.
questions.exp: The reaction reads: 'NH3 + Glutamate -(Glutamine Synthetase)-> Glutamine (Toxic)'. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: Assess the two statements on central neurochemistry in HE: I Glutamate concentration is decreased in systemic blood but increased in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). II Alzheimer type-1 cells are the classic pathological finding in hepatic encephalopathy.
questions.exp: Statement I is true ('Glutamate: ↓ in blood, ↑ in CSF'). Statement II is false because HE features Alzheimer type-2 astrocytes; Alzheimer type-1 cells occur in PMLE. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: A 50-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites develops severe confusion. Serum ammonia is markedly elevated. In the cerebral cortex, excessive glutamine accumulation within astrocytes leads to osmotic swelling and triggers secondary neuronal injury via which receptor?
questions.exp: Ammonia and glutamine toxicity leads to 'NMDA -> Secondary Neuronal damage'. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Hepatic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte pathophysiology
questions.q: In which neurological disorder are Alzheimer's type-1 cells characteristically observed according to the margin note?
questions.exp: The note states: 'Alzheimer's type-1 cell : PMLE (Aggressive multifocal Leukoencephalopathy)'. (Book p1010)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: Match each category of precipitating factors in hepatic encephalopathy with its representative examples — 1) NH3-increasing nitrogenous loads 2) Alkalosis and electrolyte drivers … A) Hypokalemia from diuretics, hypovolemia, hyponatremia, and dehydration activating RAAS B) High dietary protein, constipation, GI hemorrhage, sepsis, and blood transfusion
questions.exp: Direct NH3-increasing factors include high protein, constipation, GI hemorrhage, sepsis, and transfusion; alkalosis triggers include hypokalemia (diuretics), hypovolemia, hyponatremia, and dehydration. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: Why does metabolic alkalosis aggravate hepatic encephalopathy compared to acidosis?
opts: Alkalosis shifts the NH3 + H+ <-> NH4+ equilibrium toward uncharged NH3, facilitating non-ionic diffusion into the brain
Alkalosis irreversibly inhibits astrocytic glutamine synthetase
Alkalosis triggers rapid breakdown of hemoglobin into free iron
Alkalosis downregulates neuronal GABA-A receptor density
questions.exp: In the equilibrium NH3 + H+ <-> NH4+, acidosis drives conversion to non-diffusible ammonium (NH4+), whereas alkalosis drives uncharged, diffusible NH3 into brain tissue. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: By which mechanism do sedative drugs precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy?
opts: Inducing microvascular thrombosis in the portal vein
Blocking renal ammonium excretion in the collecting duct
questions.exp: Under precipitating factors, sedatives (CNS drugs) act via '↑ GABA'. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: Match each category of hepatic encephalopathy under the West Haven Criteria with its included stages — 1) Covert HE 2) Overt HE … A) Grade-II, Grade-III, and Grade-IV B) Minimal HE and Grade-I
questions.exp: West Haven criteria divide HE into Covert HE (minimal and Grade-I) and Overt HE (Grade-II, Grade-III, and Grade-IV). (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: A 56-year-old cirrhotic patient appears completely normal on routine clinical bedside examination with no confusion or asterixis. However, formal psychometric testing demonstrates a positive Number Connection Test. What grade of hepatic encephalopathy is present?
questions.exp: Minimal HE features a clinically normal patient whose deficit is revealed by psychometric testing, such as a positive Number Connection Test. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Grade-I hepatic encephalopathy under the West Haven Criteria?
questions.exp: Grade-I features are Anxious, Altered Sleep Pattern, and Short attention span without asterixis; asterixis emerges in Grade-II. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: Match each West Haven Grade of Overt Hepatic Encephalopathy with its defining clinical features — 1) Grade-II 2) Grade-III 3) Grade-IV … A) Semi-stupor stage, gross disorientation, bizarre behavior, responsive to pain; rigidity, clonus, hyperreflexia B) Coma; decorticate posture, triphasic waves on EEG C) Personality issues, behavioral abnormalities, disorientation; mild slurring of speech, asterixis
questions.exp: Grade-II = personality/behavior/disorientation + asterixis; Grade-III = semi-stupor/bizarre/pain-responsive + clonus/hyperreflexia; Grade-IV = coma + decorticate posture + triphasic EEG. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: At which West Haven grade does asterixis (flapping tremor) first become clinically demonstrable?
questions.exp: Asterixis is absent in Minimal and Grade-I HE and first appears as a clinical finding in Grade-II. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: Fill up: In Grade-IV hepatic encephalopathy, motor posturing manifests as ______ posture, and electroencephalography reveals bilateral synchronous triphasic waves.
questions.exp: Under Grade-IV clinical findings, the table lists 'Decorticate posture' and 'Triphasic EEG'. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: Assess the two statements on HE diagnostic signs: I Constructional apraxia in early encephalopathy is elicited by asking the patient to construct a star or matchstick pattern. II Triphasic waves on EEG are characteristically seen in Minimal hepatic encephalopathy.
questions.exp: Statement I is true as shown in the star/matchstick test. Statement II is false because triphasic waves appear in Grade-IV coma. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests
questions.q: A 62-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis presents in a semi-stuporous state with gross disorientation and bizarre outbursts. He localizes and withdraws only to deep nailbed pressure. Physical examination reveals marked cogwheel rigidity, ankle clonus, and 3+ hyperreflexia. What is his West Haven grade?
questions.exp: Semi-stupor, gross disorientation, response to pain, rigidity, clonus, and hyperreflexia define Grade-III hepatic encephalopathy. (Book p1011)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: Which pharmacological intervention is designated as the 'most important' treatment for hepatic encephalopathy?
opts: Lactulose bowel wash (4 times a day)
questions.exp: Under treatment, Lactulose Bowel wash is explicitly annotated as 'most important' with a frequency of '4 times a day'. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: What are the recommended dosing options for Rifaximin in the management of hepatic encephalopathy?
opts: 200 mg once daily or 400 mg BD
questions.exp: The treatment tree specifies Rifaximin dosing as '400mg TDS / 550 mg BD'. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: Match each pharmacological agent used in hepatic encephalopathy with its therapeutic description — 1) LOLA 2) Sodium benzoate … A) Promotes non-urea nitrogen clearance by shifting NH3 to ammonium (NH4+) excretion B) L-ornithine L-aspartate, providing substrate for residual urea cycle and glutamine synthesis
questions.exp: LOLA (L-ornithine L-aspartate) works alongside branched-chain AAs, while sodium benzoate shifts nitrogen waste via 'NH3 -> NH4+'. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: Which oral hypoglycemic agent is included among the medical therapies for hepatic encephalopathy on this page?
questions.exp: Under the treatment header, the third branch lists 'Acarbose'. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: Fill up: In the colon, bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed lactulose produces hydrogen gas and ______.
questions.exp: The diagram states: 'Lactulose fermented by colonic bacteria to H2 and VFA'. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the mechanism of action (MOA) of lactulose detailed on this page?
opts: Laxative effect promoting rapid excretion of ammonia in stool
Stimulation of canalicular MRP-2 to accelerate bile salt excretion
Reduction in luminal pH driving conversion of NH3 + H+ -> NH4+ (ammonium trapping)
Formation of volatile fatty acids as preferred substrate for bacteria, reducing ammonia synthesis
questions.exp: The three MOA points are ↓ pH (NH3 + H+ -> NH4+), volatile fatty acid formation, and laxative effect; MRP-2 canalicular stimulation is not involved. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: Why does bacterial consumption of volatile fatty acids (VFA) help reduce ammonia levels in hepatic encephalopathy?
opts: VFA accelerates renal glomerular filtration of urea
VFA stimulates hepatic sinusoidal nitric oxide production
Bacteria utilize VFA as a preferred energy substrate, suppressing their breakdown of amino acids into ammonia
VFA directly binds and neutralizes systemic GABA receptors
questions.exp: The flowchart explains: 'Bacteria use VFA as preferred substrate, thus reducing production of ammonia'. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: Assess the two statements on lactulose: I Lactulose is completely absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum before reaching the colon. II Ionized ammonium (NH4+) formed by luminal acidification cannot easily diffuse back across the colonic mucosa.
questions.exp: Statement I is false because lactulose is 'not absorbed in small intestine'. Statement II is true because ionic NH4+ is trapped in the lumen and excreted. (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: What is designated as the 'Last treatment option' for patients with refractory hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.exp: The bottom note concludes: 'Liver Transplant : Last treatment option.' (Book p1012)

questions.sec: Medical management · lactulose MOA, rifaximin and liver transplant
questions.q: A 58-year-old cirrhotic patient with recurrent Grade-II hepatic encephalopathy is managed with lactulose enemas. To further suppress ammoniagenic gut flora without inducing systemic antibiotic toxicity, non-absorbable antibiotic therapy is added. What is the standard drug and oral dosing regimen?
opts: Rifaximin 550 mg BD or 400 mg TDS
Metronidazole 400 mg TDS continuously for 1 year
Neomycin 2 g daily with weekly audiometry
questions.exp: The recommended non-absorbable antibiotic is Rifaximin dosed at 550 mg BD or 400 mg TDS. (Book p1012)

units.title: Porto-systemic encephalopathy types, neurotoxins and astrocyte swelling
units.guide: Porto-systemic encephalopathy terminology, Types A, B, and C (Type A cerebral edema m/c cause of death, Type C cirrhosis m/c), neurotoxins (ammonia, mercaptans, manganese, GABA, octopamine), colonic glutaminase, non-ionic NH3 diffusion, Alzheimer type-2 astrocytes, glutamine synthetase swelling, and distinction from PMLE type-1 cells.

units.title: Precipitating triggers, West Haven criteria and diagnostic bedside signs
units.guide: NH3-increasing triggers (protein, constipation, bleeding, sepsis), alkalosis shifting NH4+ to NH3, diuretic hypokalemia and RAAS activation, sedatives increasing GABA, West Haven covert (minimal positive number connection test, Grade-I sleep reversal) versus overt (Grade-II asterixis, Grade-III clonus/rigidity, Grade-IV decorticate triphasic EEG), and constructional apraxia.

units.title: Medical management ladder, lactulose MOA and liver transplantation
units.guide: Lactulose bowel wash 4 times daily (most important), rifaximin 400 mg TDS / 550 mg BD, acarbose, LOLA / branched-chain AA, sodium benzoate NH3 trapping, lactulose three-fold MOA (luminal acidification trapping NH4+, VFA bacterial substrate shift, osmotic laxation), and liver transplantation as final option.
